newsitem.title: UK: US payrolls hit European bonds, but spread gains.
newsitem.headline: US payrolls hit European bonds, but spread gains.

text.p: European bond markets took a hit on Friday after a stronger than expected jump in U.S. non-farm payrolls, but nevertheless managed to steal a few basis points of outperformance over Treasuries.
But analysts said with the mark buckling against the dollar, the edge may be shortlived.

"We recommended buying the U.S. versus Germany last Friday at a spread of 70 basis points with a target of 50 and we maintain that view," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets.
"Germany is under big pressure here -- the dollar has broken higher, the short end is under pressure and the five year is getting crushed as a result."
Bonds prices fell across Europe after the U.S. data, but later regained some ground.
By 1340 GMT, September Bund futures on LIFFE were at 102.83, down 20 basis points on the day but off a session low of 102.75.
September gilts were up 5/32 at 115-19 versus 115-25 before the data, while the Notionnel future on MATIF was at 130.44, down 0.42 on the day and down from 130.74 before the data.
McDevitt said a key trendline at 102.85 on the Bund chart had been broken, which opened the risk of a weaker close on Friday.

The 10-year T-note/Bund spread was at 59 basis points from 56 just before the U.S. employment data. Non-farm payrolls showed a rise of 316,000 in July, above the 193,000 expected and up from the revised 228,000 rise in June.

The mark was off its lows on the crosses but was still soft following its slump to a fresh 7-1/2-year low against the dollar amid expectations of a broader European single currency. By 1335 GMT, it was at 1.8568.

Economists said the initial tumble in bond markets was a knee-jerk reaction to the hefty headline figure, but added closer examination of the U.S. data showed little reason to sound the alarm on inflation.
Average hourly earnings were unchanged at $12.23, versus an expected 0.2 percent rise while the average weekly hours fell to 34.4 and overtime hours fell to 4.6.
"The focus is on the lack of inflationary pressure," Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London, told Reuters Financial Television.
"We have seen this combination of strong growth and little movement on hourly earnings and the working week before. The Fed will be able to refrain from raising rates in the near term."
European bond markets have enjoyed a good run recently, with a number of contracts breaking their highs, partly on the back of the growing optimism over U.S. interest rates.
McDevitt said his longer term target for the T-bond/Bund spread was still zero.
